# February 29, 1960

You arrived on a Monday that most calendars never possess — and you entered a world in 1960 that was itself balanced on an edge, two superpowers circling each other, old orders dissolving, new configurations not yet legible.

---

## The Day Itself

February 29 exists because a solar year is not 365 days but closer to 365 and a quarter, and without correction the calendar drifts — summers sliding toward autumn over the centuries. The leap day is the correction. You are one of the roughly five million people alive at any given time who share this date, and you have spent your sixty-six years navigating the small absurdity of a birthday that most years simply does not appear. Your sixteenth actual February 29 came in 2024. Your seventeenth will arrive in 2028.

---

## The Exact Day: Morocco

On the night of February 29, 1960, a shallow earthquake struck the coastal city of **Agadir, Morocco**, and much of the city ceased to exist. The tremor hit late in the evening. Buildings across the old city and the new quarters both collapsed. Somewhere between twelve and fifteen thousand people died — nearly half the city's population. The destruction was so complete that rather than rebuild on the same ground, Morocco would eventually construct a new Agadir from scratch.

Morocco had been independent from France for only four years. The disaster fell on a young nation still finding its footing, still in the first years of self-governance. King Mohammed V, who had been exiled by the French in 1953 and returned to lead independence, directed the relief effort himself.

You were born the same night this city was destroyed. That simultaneity is part of what the world handed you at the start.

---

## Sixteen Days Before: A New Nuclear Power

*On February 13, 1960 — sixteen days before you were born — France detonated its first nuclear weapon in the Algerian Sahara.*

The test, code-named Gerboise Bleue, made France the world's fourth nuclear power, after the United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain. Charles de Gaulle had been insisting for years that French security and French prestige required an independent nuclear deterrent — that France could not rely indefinitely on an American umbrella. The bomb in the desert was his answer.

The Algerian Sahara was not a neutral testing ground. France was fighting a brutal war in Algeria at that moment, attempting to hold a colony that was fighting for independence. Testing a nuclear weapon in the territory of a people simultaneously fighting to be free of French rule carried an irony that did not go unnoticed.

You were born into a world with four nuclear powers. By the time you are reading this, there are nine.

---

## 1960 as a Hinge Year

The year you were born into was one of the most consequential in postcolonial history. Seventeen African nations gained independence in 1960 alone — it became known simply as the **Year of Africa**. Belgian Congo, Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Somalia, and a dozen more: an entire continent reorganizing itself within a single calendar year. The United Nations, which had fifty-one founding members in 1945, would add sixteen new members from Africa in 1960.

The map of the world was being redrawn, and the pace of redrawing was dizzying.

Meanwhile, in the United States, Eisenhower's presidency was in its final year. A young senator from Massachusetts was running for the White House, promising something the campaign called vigor. The election that November — Kennedy vs. Nixon — would be the first in which television arguably decided the outcome. The decade the country was entering would be unlike anything it had experienced.

---

## The Arc

You are sixty-six years old now, born at the tail end of the Baby Boom, your conscious childhood shaped by the latter part of the 1960s.

You were nine when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the moon — old enough to understand what you were watching. Fourteen when Nixon resigned, seventeen when the Vietnam War ended. You came of age in the 1970s, a decade that America spent largely in a form of national hangover: Watergate, oil shocks, stagflation, the sense that the postwar confidence of the 1950s and early 1960s had been used up. You were twenty when Reagan was elected on the promise of restoring that confidence.

You were twenty-nine when the Berlin Wall fell — the Cold War that had been the background noise of your entire life suddenly switching off. You were thirty-one when the Soviet Union dissolved. The internet arrived in your early thirties. 9/11 happened at forty-one. The smartphone at forty-seven. The pandemic at sixty. And now the AI turn at sixty-six, still moving fast.

The arc from Agadir's earthquake to the present is sixty-six years of extraordinary compression. The nine nuclear powers, the seventeen-nations-in-one-year pace of decolonization, the four-country nuclear club of your birth year: all of it feels like ancient history now, which means you are old enough to remember something the present has largely forgotten.

---

## What Kind of World

February 29, 1960 was a Monday that rarely exists, struck by a disaster in Morocco and born sixteen days after a nuclear detonation in the Sahara. The year around it was reshaping the map of the planet. The decade ahead would reshape the culture of it.

You arrived on the hinge. The world before you — colonial, Cold War, confident in its settled categories — was already giving way on the night of your birth to something more complicated, more various, and considerably less certain of itself.

You have been living in that something ever since.
